short_description: N queens counting as a rare event and a quantile integral, turned into a Monte Carlo program for P versus NP: NP = RP is shown equivalent to sampling queens completions, promise RP = promise P, which implies P = RP, is restated as a hitting set problem, with exact computations on the queens.
description:
Counting the solutions of the N queens problem is a rare event probability, and a rare event probability is the integral of a quantile function on the unit interval: the Lorenz curve identity behind nested sampling and vertical likelihood Monte Carlo. This book turns that observation into a Monte Carlo program for the P versus NP problem, stated as a sequence of theorems and conjectures with the gaps marked.

Part I sets out the problem from Hilbert, Turing and Shannon to the randomized classes RP and BPP, the barriers, the exponential time hypothesis, Kolmogorov complexity and pseudorandomness. Part II is the queens: Gauss and Nauck, the rare event reformulation, Simkin's queenon, entropy and rate functions. Part III develops the machinery: product estimators, mixing times, cross entropy, Lorenz curves, vertical likelihood and its Yakowitz type error bounds, nested sampling, sequential Monte Carlo and generative Bayesian computation.

Part IV states the program. The sampling half proves that NP = RP is equivalent to polynomial time sampling and approximate counting of the completions of partial queens boards, and states as conjectures the mixing conditions under which a vertical walk on the energy levels would deliver them. The derandomization half, which gives the book its title, restates promise RP = promise P, which implies P = RP, as the known hitting set problem on the quantile axis and does not claim a proof. The book reports exact computations on the queens: the density of states, the giant component of solutions on conditioned boards, the shattering depth of the bottom level sets, and spectral gaps, all reproducible from the code in its repository, and ends with the open problems and their status.

chapters.title: The Problem in One Chapter
chapters.summary:
This opening chapter states the P versus NP problem and surveys the whole book in the form of a long essay. It explains the difference between problems that are easy to solve and problems that are easy to check, defines the classes P, NP, RP, BPP and #P informally, and tells the history from Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem through Gödel's letter of 1956 to the Millennium Prize Problem. It lists what is known, namely the three barriers (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization), the consequences of P = NP, Ladner's theorem and the hardness versus randomness theorems that make P = BPP believable. It then introduces the book's laboratory, the N queens completion problem, a #P complete counting problem with an energy given by the number of attacking pairs, and the thesis that counting and sampling can be seen through the quantile function of a level set walk (vertical likelihood Monte Carlo). The chapter summarises the findings of the later parts (connectivity of level sets, mixing of the swap chain, density of states, cross entropy and cloning methods) without proving anything new. It is a reading guide: the sampling half (NP = RP) has computations and theorems, while the derandomization half (P = RP) restates the known hitting set formulation.

chapters.title: Hilbert, Gödel and the Decision Problem

It starts with Hilbert's program (completeness, consistency and decidability of mathematics) and his tenth problem, presents Gödel's incompleteness theorems and the idea of arithmetising syntax, and asks what a mechanical procedure is. It closes with the step from computability to complexity: the bounded version of the Entscheidungsproblem (does a formula have a proof of length at most n) is in NP and NP complete, which is the question in Gödel's 1956 letter. chapters.title: Circuits and Lower Bounds
chapters.summary:
This chapter surveys Boolean circuit lower bounds, because both P versus NP and P versus BPP would most likely be settled by them. It presents Shannon's counting argument (most functions need circuits of size about 2^n/n) and the contrast with the best explicit bounds, then restricted classes: constant depth circuits (parity not in AC0, switching lemma), monotone circuits (clique, Razborov, Alon and Boppana), and modular gates (Razborov and Smolensky; Williams's separation of NEXP from ACC0). For general circuits the record is 3.1n minus lower order terms. It explains why such techniques stop (the natural proofs barrier), how hardness versus randomness needs exponential circuit lower bounds for a function in E, the partial converses of Impagliazzo, Kabanets and Wigderson and of Kabanets and Impagliazzo, and what this means for the hitting set formulation of P = RP: a derandomization would give a circuit lower bound. chapters.title: The Three Barriers
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains why P versus NP has resisted every known technique through three barrier theorems: relativization (Baker, Gill and Solovay: there are oracles making P = NP and P not equal to NP), natural proofs (Razborov and Rudich: a natural property useful against circuits contradicts pseudorandom functions) and algebrization (Aaronson and Wigderson). It sketches why each holds and which known results (interactive proofs, PCP) escape relativization by arithmetization. It then asks where the Monte Carlo program stands. The sampling half would require a mixing time bound for a concrete Markov chain, which is neither relativizing nor natural, although it must go the wrong way relative to the truth. The derandomization half, a deterministic hitting set, is a circuit lower bound by Kabanets and Impagliazzo, so all barriers apply in full. The chapter states that neither half is a proof and that the book claims neither.

chapters.title: What a Resolution Would Mean
chapters.summary:
This chapter describes the worlds in which P = NP or P is not NP and what each would mean for mathematics, cryptography, optimisation and for the Monte Carlo program. If P = NP the polynomial hierarchy collapses, optimisation and proof search become feasible, and cryptography based on one way functions fails; Levin's universal search shows constructiveness is not the issue. If P is not NP the picture is as it appears, with the status of cryptography depending on one way functions. The chapter then describes intermediate worlds in Impagliazzo's classification (Algorithmica, Heuristica, Pessiland, Minicrypt, Cryptomania), the possibilities NP in BPP, and NP in P/poly (Karp and Lipton), and the role of counting through Toda's theorem. chapters.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis
chapters.summary:

chapters.title: Interactive Proofs, Arithmetization and the PCP Theorem
chapters.summary:
This chapter covers the results that escape the relativization and natural proofs barriers by arithmetization, and what they mean for the program. It describes interactive proofs (Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff; Babai), Shamir's theorem IP = PSPACE built on the sum check protocol of Lund, Fortnow, Karloff and Nisan, and the PCP theorem (Arora, Safra, Lund, Motwani, Sudan and Szegedy; Dinur's gap amplification proof) with its equivalence to hardness of approximating MAX 3SAT. It then speculates, explicitly as suggestive rather than established, that PCP encodings correspond to an energy with a gap, and asks what would fail on hard boards: shattering and torpid mixing of the level set chain versus an empty level. chapters.title: Gauss and the Queens
chapters.summary:
The chapter introduces the N queens problem, the counting laboratory of the book. It recounts Bezzel's 1848 question, Nauck's 1850 count of 92 solutions for the eight queens board and Gauss's correspondence with Schumacher, fixes notation (a placement is a permutation of {1,...,N} with no two queens on a common diagonal), tabulates Q(N), the number of solutions, and notes the exhaustive count to N = 27 (the Q27 project). It describes the dihedral symmetry of the board, which splits the 92 solutions of the eight queens into 12 orbits, and states Simkin's asymptotics Q(N) = ((1 + o(1)) N e^{-alpha})^N with alpha about 1.942, so that a solution is an exponentially rare event among row placements and permutations. It gives three reasons for choosing the queens: a natural energy (the number of attacking pairs) with a density of states, NP completeness and sharp P completeness of the completion problem (Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale), and enough concreteness to test Monte Carlo counting on exact data. The chapter is background and states no new theorem.

chapters.title: Counting as a Rare Event
chapters.summary:
The chapter turns counting into probability. For a finite set of configurations with an energy whose zero set is the set of solutions, the number of solutions equals the size of the set times the probability that a uniform configuration has zero energy, so counting N queens becomes estimating the rare event probability rho_N = Q(N)/N^N (or Q(N)/N! on permutations). It shows why naive Monte Carlo fails, since the relative variance (1 - rho)/(M rho) forces a sample size of order 1/(epsilon^2 rho), exponential in N, and presents the embedding principle of shrinking the ambient space to the symmetric group. It tabulates the exact density of states N(s), the number of permutations with s attacking pairs, for N = 4 to 9, and introduces the Boltzmann weight, the partition function Z(gamma), and the zero temperature limit that returns the count, so that annealing, Wang and Landau and related methods become counting methods. The chapter also states the central claim of the book, that the quantile function of Monte Carlo links the physicist's entropy of states with the complexity theorist's sharp P.

chapters.title: Simkin's Theorem and the Queenon
chapters.summary:
The chapter explains how Simkin's theorem on the number of N queens solutions is proved and what its constant means. The upper bound on Q(N) comes from an entropy argument: the chain rule for entropy, applied row by row, is refined by conditioning on block occupation numbers on a coarse grid, which leads to a functional on the limit objects called queenons (permutons whose mass in each diagonal strip is at most the width of the strip). The lower bound comes from a random greedy placement analysed by the differential equations method of Wormald, with an absorption step, and the chapter reads this construction as a ladder whose rungs are the rows. It reports the authors' own enumeration of the queenon density at N = 13, which is largest near the midpoints of the edges and smallest in the corners, discusses the constant alpha = 1.942 with Simkin's bounds 1.939 to 1.945, compares it with the independence estimate 1 + 2/3, and examines finite size corrections in Q(N)/N! against data up to N = 27. chapters.title: Entropy, Types and the Rate Function of the Queens
chapters.summary:
The chapter gives the information theoretic view of the counting problem. It reviews the method of types and Sanov's theorem, extends types to permutations through block occupancy matrices (permutons as limits), and uses the entropy chain rule for a uniform random solution as a counting tool, which is the skeleton of Simkin's upper bound. It interprets the ladder of the product estimator as a decomposition of the entropy drop from permutations to solutions, about 0.94 N nats or 1.36 N bits, in the light of Shannon's source coding theorem. It defines the rate function I(e) of the number of attacking pairs of a random permutation, computes finite size versions from the exact density of states for N = 8 to 11, and states a conjecture, not proved, that I(e) exists, is convex with I(2/3) = 0 and is given by a variational problem over queenon like densities with I(0) = alpha - 1. It ends with the link between entropy and mixing (modified log Sobolev inequality, random transposition walk) and an accounting of what entropy says about the cost of the program.

chapters.title: Latin Squares and Other Permutation Counts
chapters.summary:
The chapter surveys counting problems on permutations in which a constraint removes an exponentially large fraction of the N! permutations, and compares their asymptotic constants with that of the queens. It treats derangements and board avoiding permutations, exact by inclusion exclusion through the rook polynomial; Latin squares, whose leading asymptotics log L(n) = n^2 log n - 2 n^2 + o(n^2) follow from the van der Waerden and Bregman permanent inequalities, with the lower order terms open; toroidal queens, which have no solutions unless gcd(N, 6) = 1 and whose count is ((1 + o(1)) N e^{-3})^N, matching upper and lower bounds; and the permanent of a zero one matrix. It explains why the Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda approximation scheme for the permanent covers every single permanent of the family but not the queens, whose inclusion exclusion over attacking pairs has alternating signs. It argues that the question about alpha is whether it is the value of a recognisable functional at the queenon, and states no new theorem.

chapters.title: Product Estimators and Annealing
chapters.summary:
The chapter develops the product estimator, the first of the Monte Carlo counting methods. A rare event probability rho = Z_0 is written as a telescoping product of conditional probabilities along a ladder of nested level sets of the energy, each ratio being estimated by ordinary Monte Carlo from samples conditioned on the larger level set. The variance of the product of independent unbiased estimates is computed exactly, and the chapter derives a total sample size of order T^2/epsilon^2 for a ladder of length T whose ratios are bounded below, a ladder of length O(N) for the queens being granted rather than shown. It uses the exact values for N = 8 with the density of states, and shows that the bottom ratio Z_0/Z_1 falls with N (0.094, 0.094, 0.048, 0.038 for N = 8 to 11), so the integer ladder fails the bounded ratio condition. It compares well balanced schedules, the cooling schedules of Stefankovic, Vempala and Vigoda, simulated annealing on the Boltzmann ladder, phase transitions and the cross entropy method. chapters.title: Markov Chains and Mixing Times
chapters.summary:
The chapter collects the theory of Markov chain mixing that the vertical walk relies on, since every conditioned draw of the walk is produced by a chain whose mixing time decides whether the walk is polynomial. It covers stationarity, reversibility and the Metropolis chain for the uniform distribution on a level set of the queens (swap two queens, accept if the energy stays below the level), total variation distance and mixing time, the spectral gap, conductance and Cheeger's inequality, canonical paths, coupling, and slow (torpid) mixing caused by bottlenecks. It presents the Frieze, Kannan and Polson isoperimetric analysis of the ball walk for log concave densities, as the template of a mixing proof, and a 1996 discussion paper of one author on geometric ergodicity of Gibbs and Metropolis chains. It closes by stating what mixing means for the thesis: if the mixing time is polynomial at every level the walk is an FPRAS, and for the queens completion count that would give NP = RP, while the authors believe the opposite. No new theorem is stated.

chapters.title: Convergence of MCMC and the Witch's Hat
chapters.summary:
The chapter gives the statistical side of Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence, because every level set sampler of the book is an MCMC algorithm. It describes the Gibbs sampler and the Metropolis Hastings algorithm as used in Bayesian inference, Peskun's ordering of reversible chains, the convergence theory of Tierney and of Meyn and Tweedie (geometric ergodicity, drift and small sets), a 1996 discussion paper of one of the authors on these conditions, and the diagnostics of Gelman and Rubin and of Geyer. Its central example is the witch's hat, a density on the unit cube with a narrow spike over a flat plateau, for which Gibbs and Metropolis chains can look converged by every diagnostic while being exponentially far from stationarity, because the spike carries most of the mass and is exponentially hard to find. The chapter reads the witch's hat as the bottom rung problem of the queens in miniature. No new theorem is stated.

chapters.title: Random Walks on the Symmetric Group
chapters.summary:
The swap chain on a level set of the queens is the random transposition walk on the symmetric group restricted to a subset, and this chapter presents the theory of the unrestricted walk and asks what survives the restriction. It states the exact spectrum from the representation theory of the symmetric group, the cutoff of the random transposition walk at (1/2) N log N steps (Diaconis and Shahshahani), the comparison techniques of Diaconis and Saloff Coste for transferring spectral gap bounds between reversible chains, and Fourier analysis of the energy function on permutations. It explains that the spectrum is lost on a restricted subset but comparison methods carry over and give a possible route to mixing bounds on the giant component of a level set, and discusses cutoff for the level sets. It is the group theoretic counterpart of the isoperimetric route of the volume problem. No new theorem is stated.

chapters.title: The Volume Problem and Isoperimetry
chapters.summary:
The volume of a convex body is a sharp P hard problem with a complete theory, and the chapter presents it as the model for what a mixing proof for the queens would look like. It extends the analysis to log concave densities (Applegate and Kannan; Frieze, Kannan and Polson) and reports the Kannan, Lovasz and Simonovits conjecture on the isoperimetric constant, with the reductions and bounds of Eldan, Lee and Vempala, Chen, Klartag and Lehec. chapters.title: Sampling versus Counting
chapters.summary:
The chapter states and explains the equivalence between approximate counting and approximately uniform sampling for self reducible problems, and what it means for the queens. The queens completion problem is self reducible by fixing the column of the first queen. The theorem of Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani says that for a self reducible NP relation a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) exists exactly when a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler exists, and the chapter explains why an FPRAS for an NP complete decision problem gives NP = RP. It lists successes of the method (the permanent of dense matrices and of arbitrary nonnegative matrices, the ferromagnetic Ising model, convex body volume), notes that all have decision versions in P, and discusses torpid mixing for antiferromagnetic models. It then presents the Swendsen and Wang cluster algorithm through the Edwards and Sokal joint distribution, the random cluster model, and slice sampling, proposes a slice sampling form for the repulsive queens interaction, and states that its mixing is unknown. No new theorem is stated.

chapters.title: Rare Event Simulation
chapters.summary:
The chapter reviews the theory of rare event simulation from the vertical point of view, with the queens probability P(S = 0), about e^{-0.942 N} on permutations, as the running example. chapters.title: Rubinstein's Cross Entropy Method for Counting
chapters.summary:
The chapter sets Rubinstein's methods for counting beside the vertical walk: the cross entropy method for counting, the Gibbs cloner, stochastic enumeration and Knuth's tree size estimator. Its mathematical content is a theorem on product proposals for the queens: for any importance sampling proposal of product form on the N^N row placements, the relative variance of the estimator of Q(N) is at least exp(N log N - d - log Q(N)) - 1, where d is the total entropy deficit of the one point marginals of the uniform distribution on solutions, so a product family improves on crude Monte Carlo by a factor of at most e^d in the relative second moment. Exact marginals computed for N up to 12 show that d is at most 0.68 nats, and a run of the cross entropy method collapses onto a few placements. The chapter then discusses richer sequential families and the learned sampler question, cloning and generalised splitting as a Feynman Kac estimator, Knuth's estimator as a vertical walk with no chain, and why none of these escapes the NP = RP equivalence.

chapters.title: Lorenz Curves, Majorization and Concentration

It then shows the rearrangement invariance of the vertical approach (the quantile function determines the walk, the geometry of the space only enters through the level set samplers), introduces the concentration function of Cifarelli and Regazzini, which is the Lorenz curve of a likelihood ratio and links to the Neyman and Pearson lemma, describes the product estimator as a composition of concentration functions with a kink at rho, and proves a deterministic bracket of order 1/n for Riemann sums of a monotone quantile function. chapters.title: Vertical Likelihood Monte Carlo
chapters.summary:
Can an expectation over an astronomically large space, such as the count of N queens solutions, be turned into a one dimensional integral that Monte Carlo can attack, and what does that say about derandomizing RP? This chapter develops vertical likelihood Monte Carlo, the technical core of the book. The Lorenz identity writes the evidence Z, the expectation of a nonnegative likelihood under a prior, as the integral over the unit interval of the quantile function of the likelihood. Vertical importance sampling puts a density on the quantile axis, and the choice of that density is the choice of an annealing schedule. The chapter shows how nested sampling, split sampling, the Wang Landau algorithm, the multicanonical and 1/k ensembles, and energy domain samplers sit in one framework, and it explains why Yakowitz type trapezoidal rules on ordered uniforms converge faster than naive Monte Carlo when the quantile function can be evaluated. It states plainly that sampling from the prior restricted to a likelihood level set is an oracle, as hard for the queens as NP = RP. It then reorders a randomized algorithm: the acceptance probability of an RP algorithm is a single step quantile function, and P = RP is restated as a question about medians of promise Boolean functions. The reordering relocates the randomness and does not derandomize anything, and no proof of P = RP is claimed.

chapters.title: The Algorithms of Vertical Likelihood Monte Carlo
chapters.summary:
What is the algorithm behind vertical likelihood Monte Carlo, and can it run in polynomial time? This chapter returns to the paper of Polson and Scott and sets out its algorithms one at a time. The weighted slice sampler adds a weight on the slice variable to the slice sampling joint, so that the choice of a proposal on the sample space is replaced by a choice of a weight on the likelihood axis. Special cases include the harmonic mean estimator and power posteriors, and the construction covers energy level samplers. The score heuristic gives a default weight, the truncated reciprocal of the survival function of the likelihood, and the algorithm is shown to be equivalent to nested sampling. The chapter studies mixing of the chain of likelihood ordinates, which under exact draws moves as a random walk on the log survival scale, and states a conjecture, with a heuristic argument and no complete proof, that this chain mixes in time quadratic in the log of the reciprocal rare event probability, which is order N squared for the queens. A second conjecture says the whole algorithm is polynomial exactly when the level set draws are, so for log concave problems it is polynomial and for the queens completion count it is polynomial if and only if NP = RP. Nothing here proves that equivalence unconditionally.

#### From the literature

chapters.title: Rates of Convergence in the Quantile Coordinate
chapters.summary:
How fast does integration in the quantile coordinate converge, and why is it faster than naive Monte Carlo? This chapter proves the rate claims made in the vertical likelihood chapter. The integrand is a nonincreasing function on the unit interval, the quantile function of the likelihood, and the estimator is a Riemann sum or trapezoid on n ordered uniform draws. The tool is the exact distribution of uniform spacings. For a smooth integrand the trapezoid on random ordered nodes has mean squared error of order n to the power minus 4, against n to the power minus 1 for the plain average. For a general monotone integrand the left and right Riemann sums bracket the integral and have mean squared error of order log squared n over n squared, because the error is controlled by the largest spacing. For a staircase the rate depends on the number and heights of the steps. The chapter also explains why the original coordinate, of dimension N or N squared for the queens, admits no such rate, and adds a remark on quasi Monte Carlo and low discrepancy sequences. The rates apply only when the quantile function can be evaluated at the nodes, which is the catch of the vertical walk. These bounds are sharpened in the chapters on Yakowitz bounds and exact staircase theory.

#### From the literature

The trapezoidal rule on ordered uniform draws and its mean squared error rate for smooth integrands (Yakowitz, Krimmel and Szidarovszky 1978). Trapezoidal Monte Carlo integration with random nodes (Masry and Cambanis 1990). The distribution of uniform spacings and the maximal spacing, of order log n over n, as classical facts.

chapters.title: Weighted Monte Carlo Integration: The Yakowitz Bounds
chapters.summary:
What is the exact error of the trapezoidal rule on random nodes, and what does it give for the staircases that arise in counting? This chapter gives the full Yakowitz theory for weighted Monte Carlo integration in the quantile coordinate. It sets up the integral of a nonincreasing quantile function by ordered uniform nodes, derives the exact moments of uniform spacings, and proves the Yakowitz, Krimmel and Szidarovszky trapezoidal theorem for twice continuously differentiable integrands with explicit constants: expected absolute error of order n to the power minus 2 and mean squared error of order n to the power minus 4. It extends the analysis to Lipschitz integrands and to bounded variation, with a logarithmic factor from the maximal spacing, and to staircases with K jumps, where the left and right Riemann sums bracket the integral and the root mean square error is of order K times the top height over n. The last section applies the bounds to the vertical walk and says exactly which part of its error they control: the quadrature error on one rung, and not the error of the conditioned draws or of the product across rungs. The staircase bounds carry a factor K that a later chapter removes.

#### From the literature

- [Bracketing Riemann sums and trapezoid for a staircase with K jumps](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#staircase_bracketing_bound) (Theorem 35.3, page 142; proved): For a staircase with K jumps the left and right Riemann sums bracket the integral and have mean squared error at most a constant times lambda one squared K squared over n squared, which Chapter 37 later improves. chapters.title: Beyond Yakowitz: Higher Order and Stratified Vertical Rules
chapters.summary:
What can be gained beyond the Yakowitz trapezoid in the quantile coordinate? This chapter gives three improvements, all proved with the same spacing calculus. First, interpolatory rules of degree k on the random grid have expected error of order n to the power minus (k+1) and mean squared error of order n to the power minus 2(k+1) for integrands with k+1 bounded derivatives, a gain of a factor n to the power minus 2 in mean squared error per extra derivative. Second, stratified uniforms, one node in each of n equal strata, give an unbiased estimator whose variance is bounded by the sum of squared oscillations over four n squared, which for a staircase with K jumps is smaller by a factor K than the earlier bracketing bound (a comparison of upper bounds). Third, the nested sampling estimator, with the discarded likelihoods held fixed and the latent positions given the product Beta law, has exact mean and variance, giving an exact error bar for the spacing error rather than removing it. The chapter then asks whether the spacing error of nested sampling can be beaten, and ends with a table of rates. It states what these improvements do and do not buy for counting: they improve the quadrature of a rung and leave untouched the cost of the conditioned draws.

#### From the literature

chapters.title: Exact Yakowitz Theory for Staircases
chapters.summary:
How accurate is the trapezoidal or stratified rule on a staircase, with constants that do not depend on the number of steps? This chapter gives an exact theory for the quadrature of a nonincreasing quantile function with random ordered nodes. The key is an exact representation of the trapezoid error as an integral of the signed distance to the midpoint of the containing spacing against the jump measure of the integrand. This reduces everything to the moments of that distance, which have closed forms. The consequences are the exact bias and mean squared error for a single step, a bound of order V squared over n squared for any integrand of bounded variation V with no logarithm and no dependence on the number of steps, an asymptotic constant equal to the sum of squared jump heights over 2 n squared for separated steps, and a variance bound over 4 n squared for the stratified rule. For the Boltzmann staircase of the queens, with geometric step heights, the root mean square error of a rung is at most 0.71 over n for the trapezoid and 0.5 over n for the stratified rule, whatever N. Computations at N = 8 and 10 on the exact density of states check the bounds. The chapter says the relative error still carries the unbounded factor of the rung integral, so the cost of the walk is not changed.

#### From the literature

The trapezoidal rule on random ordered nodes and its error for smooth integrands (Yakowitz, Krimmel and Szidarovszky 1978). Uniform spacings and their moments as classical facts. Stratified sampling as the standard variance reduction.

chapters.title: Nested Sampling: The Theory
chapters.summary:
What does the theory of nested sampling say about its accuracy, and how is it a vertical walk? This chapter gives the algorithm precisely: keep n live points drawn from the prior restricted to the region above the current likelihood level, discard the worst, replace it by a draw from the constrained prior, and sum the discarded likelihoods against the geometric grid of prior mass. It proves the shrinkage lemma, that the prior mass above the worst of n live points shrinks by a factor with the Beta(n,1) law of the maximum of n uniforms, independently of the likelihood. From this it derives the error in the number of live points, discusses the choice of that number and the stopping rule, and states consistency and asymptotic normality of the log evidence estimate under the regularity conditions of Chopin and Robert, with an explicit asymptotic variance in terms of the quantile function. It covers variants, importance nested sampling and dynamic nested sampling, and the consistency of the plug in estimate on a staircase. The cost sits in the constrained draws: the number of steps is about n times the log of the reciprocal prior mass, polynomial for the queens, and the constrained draw is the hard part.

chapters.title: Sequential Monte Carlo and Feynman Kac Models
chapters.summary:
How does the theory of sequential Monte Carlo describe the vertical walk with a population of particles? This chapter places the ladder of level sets in the Feynman Kac framework of Del Moral, where the walk is a sequence of potentials and Markov kernels, the particles are resampled at each rung, and the estimate of the normalising constant is unbiased. It states the unbiasedness and central limit theorems for the particle estimate with multinomial resampling and an explicit asymptotic variance, a sum over rungs. It shows how the variance decomposes rung by rung and isolates the contribution of the sampler at each rung, which separates the Bernoulli part of the product estimator from the error of the kernels. It treats adaptive levels chosen by a quantile rule, for which the unbiasedness theorem does not apply directly but consistency and asymptotic normality hold, and genealogies and coalescence of ancestral lines, with the bottom rung of the queens as the place where failure of mixing would show. It explains what this adds to the Yakowitz and nested sampling analyses: a law of large numbers in the number of particles for the whole walk.

chapters.title: Bayesian Evidence as Counting
chapters.summary:
Is Bayesian evidence computation the same problem as counting? Vertical likelihood Monte Carlo was invented for the marginal likelihood, the expectation of the likelihood under the prior, and this chapter closes the loop. The evidence is the integral of the quantile function of the likelihood under the prior, so with an indicator likelihood on a discrete space it is a count over the size of the space, and with a Boltzmann weight it is a partition function. The standard estimators of the evidence are shown to be choices within the vertical framework: the harmonic mean estimator, thermodynamic integration over power posteriors, annealed importance sampling, and nested sampling. Posterior sampling becomes level set sampling by the slice sampling construction, and the complexity of the evidence is that of the level set draw: polynomial for log concave likelihood and prior, and as hard as the counting problem in general. The chapter restates the thesis of the program in Bayesian terms, discusses the horseshoe prior for sparse regression as a heuristic case with no mixing result claimed, and treats model selection over combinatorial model spaces as counting. No new theorem is proved.

#### From the literature

Slice sampling with auxiliary variables (Damien, Wakefield and Walker 1999). Nested sampling (Skilling 2006). Vertical likelihood Monte Carlo as a unifying view of evidence estimators (Polson and Scott 2015). Polynomial time sampling from log concave distributions by the ball walk (Frieze, Kannan and Polson 1994; Applegate, Kannan and Polson 1990). The harmonic mean estimator, thermodynamic integration and annealed importance sampling as standard methods.

chapters.title: Generative Bayesian Computation for Vertical Counting
chapters.summary:
Can generative Bayesian computation implement vertical counting? Generative Bayesian computation, GBC, represents a posterior or target distribution by a generator, a map from base noise to the target learned from simulated pairs by quantile regression, and the quantile function is also the central object of the vertical walk. This chapter shows how a learned level set generator gives a practical implementation of the ladder of level sets with no Markov chain steps. It states three theorems for finite spaces: the representation theorem, that the quantile function of the likelihood and the generator of each level set exist and are unique up to null sets under a fixed order; the estimation theorem, a Dvoretzky Kiefer Wolfowitz type bound for the empirical quantile function, whose integral is exactly the sample mean; and the amortised ladder theorem, bounding the relative mean squared error of the product estimator when each rung generator has total variation error delta. It says what generators cannot do, since a generator trained on a trapped chain inherits the trap, and ends with a section on monads, Markov categories and functors that places the Monte Carlo and derandomization halves on one axis. The chapter does not prove that a generator can be learned in polynomial time.

chapters.title: Sufficient Statistics for the Queens
chapters.summary:
Is there a sufficient statistic for the N queens problem, and what does it cost to compute? The chapter answers in three readings. For the Boltzmann family on placements, the energy, the number of attacks, is minimal sufficient for the temperature and the density of states determines the family. For the completion problem, with a partial board as data and the completions as the unknown, the minimal sufficient statistic is the closure, the set of squares occupied by every completion, and the posterior mean matrix, the summary statistic that Jiang and Wong proposed for approximate Bayesian computation, is sufficient too, for every self reducible problem. The cost is the finding: deciding membership in the closure is coNP hard, the exact matrix is sharp P hard, and approximating it to relative accuracy one over N squared in randomized polynomial time is equivalent to NP = RP. Theorems on learned generators show that a uniform generator conditioned on a summary forces sufficiency, that a product over rows pays the mean field gap, and that planted pair training weights boards by their number of completions and rarely shows the hard ones. Forced squares on random boards are tabulated. The chapter states that it does not establish NP = RP, and that no argument in the book does.

#### From the literature

Sufficient statistics, the Fisher Neyman factorisation, and minimality (Lehmann and Scheffe 1950). Learning summary statistics for approximate Bayesian computation by a deep network, with the posterior mean as summary (Jiang, Wu, Zheng and Wong 2017). Semi automatic approximate Bayesian computation (Fearnhead and Prangle 2012). Approximate Bayesian computation with Kullback Leibler divergence as discrepancy (Jiang, Wu and Wong 2018). Uniform generation and self reducibility (Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani 1986).

chapters.title: The Monte Carlo Program for P versus NP
chapters.summary:
This chapter lays out the Monte Carlo program for P versus NP as a chain of five links, each a theorem, a conjecture or an experiment, running from the Lorenz identity for the partition function to the question whether P = NP. The objects are the queens completion problem, the energy given by the number of attacking pairs, the quantile function of the Boltzmann likelihood (a staircase with at most binomial(N,2)+1 steps), the vertical walk, ladder of nested level sets, level set sampler, and the product estimator. The central statement is a conditional FPRAS theorem: if a level set sampler is available, the ladder has at most 2K rungs and consecutive size ratios are at least one half, then the vertical walk with stratified quadrature estimates the ground state count N(0) within relative error epsilon with probability at least 3/4, in time O(K^2 epsilon^-2 C(N, epsilon/K)). The chapter separates what is proved (links one to three), what is conjectured (rapid mixing of the level set chain, and P = RP in vertical form), and what is a sketch (a conditional FPRAS for the unconditioned count Q(N)). It states plainly that it does not claim to resolve P versus NP, and lists the next steps: the shattering depth of reduction boards, a cluster chain with provable properties, and explicit hitting sets.

#### From the literature

- NP completeness of queens completion and #P completeness of counting completions (Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale 2017).
- Equivalence of approximate counting and almost uniform sampling for self reducible problems (Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani 1986).
- Approximate counting is in BPP with an NP oracle (Stockmeyer 1985).
- The derandomization hypothesis P = RP and the circuit lower bound hypothesis (Impagliazzo and Wigderson 1997).
- Quadrature bounds for weighted Monte Carlo integration (Yakowitz, Krimmel and Szidarovszky 1978).
- Nested sampling and its shrinkage error (Skilling 2006; Chopin and Robert 2010).

#### New results

- [Conditional FPRAS for the vertical walk with stratified quadrature](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#conditional_fpras_vertical_walk) (Theorem 43.1, page 185; conditional on a level set sampler producing, in time C(N, delta), a sample within total variation delta of uniform on every sublevel set; the ladder hypothesis, that the ladder has at most 2K rungs and consecutive rung size ratios at least one half; for the optimality remark only, for the optimality remark only, that relative error epsilon in the product requires relative error of order epsilon over the square root of K in each rung ratio, which the book assumes and does not prove): Given a level set sampler and a ladder of at most 2K rungs with ratios at least one half, the vertical walk with stratified quadrature approximates the ground state count in time K squared over epsilon squared times the sampler cost, so counting reduces to level set sampling. New in this book.
- [FPRAS for the unconditioned queens count under mixing hypotheses (sketch)](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#fpras_unconditioned_queens_count_sketch) (Proposition 43.2, page 187; conditional on the sublevel set of energy at most 2 is connected under swaps; polynomial mixing time of the swap chain on every sublevel set of energy at most m for every m at least 2; consecutive ratios of the sublevel sets on the integer ladder are at least inverse polynomial in N; polynomial mixing of the swap chain on the giant component of the sublevel set of energy at most 1, with a membership test and with the giant component holding all but an N to the minus c fraction of the solutions; closing the two gaps the book names in its proof sketch (ratios only inverse polynomial instead of at least one half, and no bound on the size of the giant component relative to the sublevel set)): Under connectivity and polynomial mixing hypotheses for the swap chain on the unconditioned queens, an FPRAS for the number of solutions would follow; the book gives only a sketch with two acknowledged gaps. chapters.title: The Quantile Reordering of a Randomized Algorithm
chapters.summary:
This chapter turns the machinery of vertical likelihood on the complexity classes. A randomized polynomial time algorithm A(x, r) with random string r has an acceptance probability that is an expectation, and the expectation is the integral of a quantile function. Taking the likelihood to be the indicator of acceptance, the quantile reordering of the algorithm is a step function with a single step, whose location is the acceptance probability p(x). For a language in RP with acceptance probability above one half, deciding membership is evaluating the quantile function at the median, and P = RP is equivalent to a statement that the median of a Boolean function that is either identically zero or true on more than half of the random strings is computable in deterministic polynomial time. The chapter then examines in what sense the nested sampling walk is a hitting set, concluding that it is not: it is a randomized hitting set generator whose randomness sits in the level set sampler, so reordering changes where the randomness lives and does not remove it. It places derandomization of RP and approximate counting of #P on one axis, the density of states as the widths of a monotone step function. It does not resolve P versus RP.

- Counting accepting computations is complete for #P (Valiant 1979).
- The hitting set formulation of derandomization (Andreev, Clementi and Rolim 1998).
- Approximate counting is in BPP with an NP oracle (Stockmeyer 1985) and the Jerrum Valiant Vazirani correspondence between counting and sampling (Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani 1986).
- The one sided error class RP and amplification of acceptance probability.

chapters.title: Vertical Likelihood and P = RP
chapters.summary:
This chapter states precisely what vertical likelihood sampling proves about P and RP, what it would prove under natural conjectures, and what the conjectures are. A level set sampler produces near uniform samples from the sublevel sets of an energy. Under the hypothesis that such a sampler exists and consecutive level set ratios are at least inverse polynomial, the vertical likelihood walk with the integer ladder gives an FPRAS for the ground state count, with O(K^2 q epsilon^-2) samples. Applied to the queens energy on partially filled boards this yields NP = RP, a conditional statement whose hypotheses nobody has proved and which the authors regard as unlikely. Unconditionally the chapter records two standard facts: the nested sampling walk locates the single step of an RP algorithm's quantile function with the shrinkage error of nested sampling, and the Boltzmann partition function is the integral of a step function with at most K + 1 steps, with the trapezoidal rule in the quantile coordinate having mean squared error at most V^2 over 2(n+1)(n+2). It then states three conjectures in vertical form (P = RP, prBPP = prP, and a queens conjecture on the absence of a polynomial level set sampler). The authors say explicitly that they do not claim to prove P = RP; the contribution is a viewpoint.

chapters.title: Approximate Counting in the Polynomial Hierarchy
chapters.summary:
This chapter presents approximate counting within the polynomial hierarchy and places it against the vertical walk. It states Stockmeyer's theorem, that every #P function can be approximated within a factor of 1 plus or minus epsilon by a randomized polynomial time algorithm with an NP oracle (so approximate counting is in BPP with an NP oracle and in the third level of the hierarchy), and explains the proof by pairwise independent hashing, over affine maps on GF(2), and Chebyshev's inequality. The hashing ladder halves the fibre at each step, a vertical walk with ratio one half in which the NP oracle plays the role of the level set sampler. The chapter also discusses Sipser's hashing and the Valiant Vazirani isolation lemma, and the counting of satisfying assignments of a DNF formula by the Karp and Luby sampling scheme, which has an FPRAS because the embedding ratio is at least 1/k. It sketches Toda's theorem that the polynomial hierarchy lies in P with a #P oracle, and locates the queens completion count: exactly #P complete, approximately in BPP with an NP oracle, and with an FPRAS if and only if NP = RP. It states that the ladder length, rung variance and sampling cost are the three sources of difficulty in FPRAS design.

chapters.title: Phase Transitions and the Density of States
chapters.summary:
This chapter examines the staircase of the Boltzmann likelihood for the N queens problem and asks where along the quantile axis the difficulty of counting concentrates. For permutations of size N the quantile function has heights e^-s and widths N(s)/N!, where N(s) is the density of states, the number of permutations with s attacking pairs. For N = 8 the chapter reads off the widths from the exact density of states, finds that the steps s = 3 to 6 hold 69 percent of permutations, and that the ratio Z_0/Z_1 = 0.094 is the hardest. A heuristic with independent diagonal pairs gives mean energy about 2N/3 and a Poisson ground step width e^{-2N/3}, larger than Simkin's e^{-0.942 N}, and the deficit is read as the queenon correction. Exact enumeration shows the ratios N(1)/N(0) and N(2)/N(1) growing with N for N = 8 to 11. The chapter discusses where level set sampling by swap moves would fail, namely level sets that are disconnected under local moves on partially filled boards, the mechanism by which NP hardness would appear in Monte Carlo, and states that a failure to mix appears in the quantile coordinate as a wrongly estimated width.

#### From the literature

chapters.title: Numerical Experiments
chapters.summary:
This chapter reports three numerical experiments on the N queens counting problem. First, the split sampling ladder with population 400, quantile fraction 0.3 and 4N Metropolis swaps per rung, run ten times at each N from 8 to 16, estimating Q(N) within a factor 1.25 of the exact count at every N with coefficient of variation between 0.13 and 0.5 and between five and nine rungs. Second, the Wang Landau algorithm for the whole density of states at N = 10, compared with exhaustive enumeration of all 3,628,800 permutations, with relative error below 1 percent for energies 2 to 7 and 11 percent at the ground state (642 against 724). Third, a reading of the ladder itself, showing that the final ratio Z_0/Z_1 decreases with N and that the bottom rung is the hardest. The chapter states what the experiments do and do not show: the ladder works at sizes where counts can be checked, polynomial cost is by design over N up to 16, and the experiments cannot speak to the limit of large N. These are computations, with exact values known to N = 27, and not proofs of a polynomial algorithm.

chapters.title: A Cluster Chain for the Queens
chapters.summary:
This chapter designs a Swendsen Wang style cluster chain for the N queens level sets and asks what would make it mix rapidly. The queens energy is a sum of pairwise interactions between row variables, a Potts like model on the complete graph with the extra constraint that columns are distinct. An Edwards Sokal bond augmentation is written for the pairwise weights, and the conditional update of the permutation given the bonds is shown to be a hard sampling problem, unlike the Potts model. The tractable alternative is a block Gibbs chain that resamples a random block of rows uniformly among block permutations keeping the energy at most m. A proposition shows that the block chain is reversible with respect to the uniform distribution on the level set and irreducible when the level set is connected under block moves. The chapter argues, without proof, that for the completion problem the conductance may be exponentially small, since cluster moves of the queens are not correlated with any domain structure. It states a conjecture that the block chain mixes in polynomial time on unconditioned boards and superpolynomially on boards from the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction.

chapters.title: Numerical Experiments II: The Bottom Rung
chapters.summary:
This chapter measures the mixing of the swap chain on the bottom level set {S <= 1} of the N queens energy for unconditioned boards, for N in 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28 and 32. From a solution found by a min conflicts heuristic, the chain is run for 4000N proposed swaps and the integrated autocorrelation time of the first row column is estimated from six independent runs at each N. The autocorrelation time grows from 59 swaps at N = 8 to about 900 at N = 32, with a power law fit of exponent 1.76. The fraction of time at energy zero, an estimate of the bottom ratio Z_0/Z_1, falls from 0.094 to about 0.015, with the product with N between 0.4 and 0.75, consistent with decay like 1/N and no positive limit. The chapter extrapolates a cost near N^5 for the whole vertical walk on unconditioned boards, explicitly as an extrapolated estimate and not a demonstrated polynomial algorithm. It says that nothing here concerns hard reduction boards, where the NP hardness would sit, and proposes running the chain on boards from the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction as the next experiment.

chapters.title: Numerical Experiments III: Genealogies
chapters.summary:
This chapter uses the genealogy of a particle system as a diagnostic for shattered level sets. In the split sampling sampler with M = 400 particles, each initial particle carries an ancestor label through selection and mutation, and the number of distinct ancestors among the elite at each rung is recorded. It is compared with a neutral model, A_{t+1} = A_t (1 - (1 - f)^{M/A_t}), in which selection alone causes coalescence. The runs cover unconditioned queens at N = 10, 14, 18 and 22 and randomly conditioned boards at N = 14 and 18. The observed counts track the neutral prediction with a one sided shortfall of 10 to 20 percent in the middle rungs; the bottom rung at N = 18 has 4 ancestors against 8 predicted, which a diagnostic of this resolution cannot distinguish from fluctuation. The chapter notes that the equal family size formula is an upper bound on the neutral expectation, so the comparison cannot separate structure from bias, and that M in the thousands is needed for N above 20. The experiment on hard reduction boards, where an overlap gap structure should show collapse of ancestry, is not done.

chapters.title: Other Laboratories
chapters.summary:
This chapter applies the vertical view to five other hard counting problems: the permanent, the ferromagnetic Ising model, the volume of a convex body, satisfying assignments and linear extensions of a partial order. For each it describes the staircase, the level set sampler and the status of mixing. The permanent is #P complete (Valiant 1979), with an FPRAS by Jerrum and Sinclair 1989 for dense matrices and Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda 2004 for all nonnegative matrices. The Ising model has an FPRAS by Jerrum and Sinclair, and the chapter discusses Glauber and Swendsen Wang dynamics, and hardness thresholds by Sly. Convex body volume is handled by Dyer, Frieze and Kannan 1991 with improvements to the running time. For SAT the clustering transition of random constraint satisfaction is the mixing conjecture made concrete. Linear extensions are counted by a coupling argument. The pattern the authors report is that the walk is polynomial exactly for the problems with decision versions in P, while for NP complete problems the bottom rungs shatter into pieces that no efficient chain connects; this is a heuristic reading and not a theorem.

chapters.title: Average Case Hardness and the Overlap Gap Property
chapters.summary:
Does the worst case hardness of the queens completion problem say anything about the random boards on which the Monte Carlo program is tested? This chapter sets the queens against average case complexity: Levin's distributional NP completeness and Heuristica versus Pessiland, the clustering (shattering) transition in random k SAT, and the overlap gap property (OGP) as a geometric obstruction that defeats stable algorithms, including local algorithms, low degree polynomials, approximate message passing and bounded time Langevin dynamics. It defines the overlap of two queens solutions as the fraction of rows on which they agree and argues, from the exact computations of the open problems chapter, that the unconditioned queens have a giant component under swaps through near solutions and therefore no overlap gap at the sizes computed. It conjectures that this holds for every N, and expects, without proof, that boards from the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction of hard random formulas inherit an overlap gap. It poses a random queens completion model (fix a fraction of queens, find the shattering threshold) as an open problem. The chapter proves nothing new: it is a literature survey with a conjecture and a problem.

chapters.title: The Other Hypothesis: The Case for NP = RP
chapters.summary:
What is the best case that NP = RP, and does anything measured in the book contradict it? This chapter states the opposing hypothesis as its defenders would, and says the authors do not hold it. The argument from the data lists the polynomial looking quantities: bottom rung autocorrelation time growing like N^1.8 to N = 32, relaxation time of the swap chain growing like N^3 to N = 12, a giant component of the bottom level set, near solution paths of bounded length. The argument from structure says the queens have no random constraints, and compares the swap chain with the Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda proof for the permanent. The argument from complexity theory says that NP different from RP is a belief, not a theorem, and recalls the barriers (relativization, natural proofs, algebrization). The argument from the main equivalence says NP = RP needs only one mixing sampler. The chapter ends with the experiments the defenders would run (shattering depth of a reduction board) and the authors' reply. No theorem is proved.

chapters.title: A Worked Example: The Eight Queens by Every Method

chapters.title: Towards a Mixing Proof on Unconditioned Boards
chapters.summary:
Does the swap chain on the bottom level set of the unconditioned N queens mix in polynomial time, and what would a proof need? The chain moves by swapping the columns of two rows and stays inside the set of permutations with at most one attacking pair, restricted to the giant swap component G_N. The chapter states the mixing conjecture, proves elementary facts (reversibility, irreducibility, aperiodicity for N at least 8, and that swapping two rows of a solution creates at most four attacks), reports exact measurements that replace two earlier conjectures (repairable swaps per solution, distance from near solutions to solutions, spectral gap and relaxation times for N = 8 to 12), and proves a reduction by Cheeger's inequality: the mixing conjecture is equivalent to a polynomial lower bound on the conductance of G_N, the expansion conjecture. It discusses canonical paths and comparison with a block chain as possible routes and compares the problem with the KLS conjecture. The mixing and expansion conjectures remain open.

chapters.title: The Completion Problem
chapters.summary:
What changes when some queens are already placed? The queens completion problem asks for the number Q(N; X_0) of solutions extending a partial placement X_0, or whether one exists. This chapter shows that the Lorenz identity, the vertical walk, the ladder and the trapezoidal rule go through with the uniform law on the completions in place of the uniform law on permutations, so that only the sampler changes. The chapter describes that reduction from satisfiability (the partial placement encodes the clauses by blocked squares), the self reducibility of completion, which makes search polynomially equivalent to decision and brings in the Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani sampling to counting equivalence, and the vertical walk on a partial board. It records the consequence that a polynomial level set sampler for completions would give NP = RP, and that failure of the chain on reduction boards is expected.

chapters.title: Rigorous Theorems on P, NP and RP
chapters.summary:
Which rigorous statements about P, NP and RP does the vertical approach yield? This chapter collects them and says clearly that none resolves P versus NP. The main equivalence says that NP = RP is equivalent to a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler for completions of a partial queens placement, to a sampler for the level sets of the queens energy on partial boards, and to an FPRAS for the number of completions; the proof assembles Bellare, Goldreich and Petrank, Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani and the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction. The derandomization half restates the known hitting set formulation: prRP = prP is equivalent to deterministic computation of a point in, or the median of, a dense set, and under the Impagliazzo and Wigderson hypothesis P = RP; this is a coordinate change and not a proof of P = RP. The chapter also proves that no Monte Carlo method decides, approximates or samples the queens completion problem unless NP = RP, a conditional FPRAS with explicit rates in terms of the relaxation time, and a trivial vertical hitting set lemma.

#### From the literature

Uniform generation of NP witnesses with an NP oracle (Bellare, Goldreich and Petrank 2000); random generation and approximate counting (Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani 1986); NP complete queens completion (Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale 2017); P = BPP from exponential circuit lower bounds (Impagliazzo and Wigderson 1997); NP in BPP implies NP = RP (Ko 1982); one sided versus two sided error (Buhrman and Fortnow 1999).

- [Median form of the hitting set characterisation of prRP = prP](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#derandomization_equivalence_prrp_prp) (Theorem 58.2, page 244; conditional on the extension to promise problems of the Buhrman and Fortnow theorem, that prRP = prP implies prBPP = prP (used only for (1) implies (2))): A restatement on the quantile axis of the known hitting set formulation, saying that promise RP equals promise P exactly when a point with value one, or the median, of a polynomial time Boolean function can be found deterministically under the promise. It rests on the Buhrman and Fortnow theorem, assumed here to extend to promise problems. New in this book.
- [Limits of Monte Carlo for the queens completion problem](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#limits_of_monte_carlo_for_queens) (Theorem 58.5, page 245; proved): No one sided error decision algorithm, polynomial factor approximation of the completion count, or sampler within constant total variation distance runs in polynomial time unless NP equals RP. - [Conditional FPRAS with explicit rates for the stratified vertical walk](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#conditional_fpras_explicit_rates) (Theorem 58.6, page 245; proved): For an energy with K plus one levels and reversible lazy level set chains with relaxation time at most t star, the stratified vertical walk estimates the ground state count with a number of chain steps given by an explicit bound, assuming the ratios of the product estimator are bounded below. chapters.title: Lean Statements of the Main Results
chapters.summary:
Can the main results be stated in a proof assistant? This chapter is an untested sketch, not a machine checked formalization. It writes, in Lean 4 in the style of Mathlib, statements of the Lorenz identity (the layer cake formula in quantile form), the variance bound for the product estimator, the stratified quadrature bound, the main equivalence NP = RP and its sampler forms, and the vertical form of prRP = prP. The text says the code is pseudo Lean, has not been typechecked, leaves several identifiers undefined, and leaves most proofs as sorry. The chapter explains why formalizing is worth doing (it forces the definitions of a polynomial level set sampler, of total variation for a sampler that may fail, and of the promise into the open), comments on how the statements match Mathlib's probability and measure theory, and ends with the state of the project. It proves no mathematical result and verifies none by machine.

chapters.title: Open Problems: Status and Approaches
chapters.summary:
What is open in the program, and what has moved? This chapter is the working document of the book. For each problem it gives the statement, what is known, what the authors computed while writing, promising approaches and the bearing on the thesis. Problems on the structure of the queens landscape: the limit of N(0)/N(1), connectivity of solutions under swaps, the repair neighbourhood, the finite size correction to Simkin's asymptotics, the queenon and the Lorenz curve, mixing of the bottom rung, a random queens completion model and its threshold, the absence of a thermal phase transition. Problems on the vertical method: optimal vertical weight, rates in the quantile coordinate, two sided promises, hashing versus walking. Derandomization: vertical hitting sets, deterministic level set hitting. Broader program: the Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani gap, Lean and the queens. Later rounds add the shattering depth of a board (with a rung skipping theorem), the spectral gap, depth growth and Markov window families. A final section records which problems changed status, with the exact computations to N = 13 and N = 17 that support the giant component.

#### From the literature

Simkin's asymptotics for the number of queens configurations (Simkin 2023) and the queenon; random generation and approximate counting (Jerrum, Valiant and Vazirani 1986); the permanent (Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda 2004); the queens completion reduction (Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale 2017); Wang and Landau (2001) and nested sampling (Skilling 2006) as context for the vertical method.

#### New results

- [Rung skipping, the walk that starts at a connected level set](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#rung_skipping) (Theorem 60.20, page 264; conditional on the swap chain on every sublevel set of energy at most j, for j at least m, is irreducible and mixes in polynomial time T; the rung ratios are at least 1/q(N) for a polynomial q; the ratio of the number of ground states to the size of the sublevel set at m is at least 1/p(N) for a polynomial p): If a connected, well mixed sublevel set is reached at some depth m with polynomial rung ratios and a polynomial ground state fraction, the vertical walk need not use the bottom rung and gives an FPRAS for the completion count. New in this book.
- [Shattering depth on hard boards](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#shattering_depth_conjecture) (Conjecture 60.21, page 266; open): On boards built from hard formulas by the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction the shattering depth is conjectured to grow linearly in N, so that the ground state ratio at that depth is exponentially small. New in this book.
- [Depth growth on random boards](https://vsokolov.org/books/p_equals_rp/results.html#depth_growth_conjecture) (Conjecture 60.25, page 269; open): On random boards with a fixed number of fixed queens the shattering depth is conjectured to stay bounded, so that the price of rung skipping is inverse polynomial, against the alternatives of logarithmic or linear growth. New in this book.
