results.name: ETH and the program (exponential lower bounds for samplers on hard boards)
results.status_text: conditional on the hypothesis that the class E of problems decidable in time 2^{O(n)} contains a problem with no circuits of size 2^{epsilon n} for some epsilon > 0 (parts 1 and 2); the exponential time hypothesis (part 2); the randomized exponential time hypothesis, that 3 satisfiability has no randomized algorithm of time 2^{delta n} for some delta > 0 (part 3)
results.conditions: the hypothesis that the class E of problems decidable in time 2^{O(n)} contains a problem with no circuits of size 2^{epsilon n} for some epsilon > 0 (parts 1 and 2); the exponential time hypothesis (part 2); the randomized exponential time hypothesis, that 3 satisfiability has no randomized algorithm of time 2^{delta n} for some delta > 0 (part 3)
results.summary: Under the circuit hardness hypothesis of Impagliazzo and Wigderson, P equals RP, and under the exponential time hypothesis as well, P = RP and both differ from NP; under a randomized exponential time hypothesis every sampler and every FPRAS for completion counts of queens boards built from hard formulas needs exponential time for infinitely many sizes.
results.statement: Write E for the class of problems decidable in time $2^{O(n)}$. (1) (Impagliazzo and Wigderson 1997, cited, not proved in the book) If E contains a problem with no circuits of size $2^{\epsilon n}$ for some $\epsilon > 0$, then $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{BPP}$, hence $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{RP}$. (2) Assume the exponential time hypothesis (ETH) and the hypothesis of (1). Then $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{RP} = \mathrm{BPP} \ne \mathrm{NP}$, and consequently the queens level sets on the boards of the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction admit no polynomial time sampler, and no fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) for completion counts exists. The Monte Carlo half fails on hard boards for samplers and approximation schemes; the book does not prove the corresponding statement for particular realisations of the vertical walk. (3) Assume the randomized exponential time hypothesis: there is $\delta > 0$ such that 3 satisfiability has no randomized algorithm of time $2^{\delta n}$. Then on the reduction boards of a 3CNF formula with $n$ variables, every randomized algorithm that samples completions within a polynomial factor of uniform, and every FPRAS for the completion count, has running time $2^{\Omega(n)}$ for infinitely many $n$.
results.label: thm:ethprogram

results.name: A Schoening walk for the queens
results.summary: A Schoening type random walk repairing attacking pairs finds a queens completion in expected time at most (2f)^f times a polynomial in the number f of free rows, which is worse than exhaustive search.
results.statement: Consider the chain on placements of a board with $f \ge 2$ free rows (permutations of the free columns) which, from a placement with at least one attacking pair, picks an attacking pair uniformly, picks one of its two queens uniformly, the free one if the other is fixed, and swaps that queen's row with a uniformly random other free row. Started from a uniform random placement of the free rows and run for $f$ steps with restarts, the chain finds a completion, if one exists, in expected time at most $(2 f)^{f} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(f)$.
results.label: prop:schoening_queens

results.name: Coding theorem for the queens
results.summary: NP equals RP exactly when the completions of every queens board can be encoded and decoded in randomized polynomial time at their information content, the logarithm of the completion count up to a logarithmic term.
results.statement: Let $Q(N; X_0)$ be the number of completions of the partial placement $X_0$ on the $N \times N$ board. The following are equivalent. (1) $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$. (2) There is a constant $c$ and a randomized polynomial time encoder and decoder pair, sharing a random string $\sigma$ of polynomial length, with the following properties on every board $X_0$ with $Q(N; X_0) \ge 1$. With probability at least $1 - 2^{-N^2}$ over $\sigma$, every completion $x$ is encoded by a binary string of a common length $L = L(X_0, \sigma)$, computable in polynomial time from $X_0$ and $\sigma$, with $L \le \log_2 Q(N; X_0) + c \log_2 N$, and decoded correctly. For every $\sigma$, the decoder outputs only completions or a failure symbol, and at most $N^c$ strings of length $L$ decode to any one completion.
results.label: thm:coding

results.name: Existence and form of the rate function of the attack count
results.summary: The large deviation rate function of the number of attacking pairs of a random permutation is conjectured to exist, be convex with its zero at 2/3, and be given near zero by a variational problem over queenon like densities.
results.statement: The rate function $I(e)$ exists, is convex on $[0, \infty)$ with $I(2/3) = 0$, and is given near $e = 0$ by a variational problem over queenon like densities with prescribed attack density $e$ (queenons proper have $e = 0$). Heuristically $I(e) = -\sup\{ \Psi(f) : f \text{ a queenon with attack density } e \}$ for the functional $\Psi$ of Simkin's upper bound, suitably extended, so that $I(0) = \alpha - 1$. Here $e$ is the energy density $S/N$, the number of attacking pairs per queen, and the widths of the energy levels satisfy $N(s)/N! = \exp(-N I(s/N) + o(N))$. The book does not prove this.
results.label: conj:ratefn

results.name: Product proposals for the queens
results.summary: No importance sampling proposal with independent coordinates can beat crude Monte Carlo for counting N queens by more than a factor given by the entropy deficit of the solution marginals, which is small for N up to 12.
results.statement: Let $N$ be a positive integer, let $\mathcal{X}^* \subseteq [N]^N$ be the set of solutions of the $N$ queens problem among row placements, with $Q(N) = |\mathcal{X}^*|$, and let $\pi^*$ be the uniform distribution on $\mathcal{X}^*$. For $i = 1, \dots, N$ let $H_i$ be the entropy of the $i$th coordinate (the column of the queen in row $i$) under $\pi^*$, let $d_i = \log N - H_i \ge 0$ and $d = \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i$. For any proposal distribution $g$ on $[N]^N$ of product form, $g(x) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} g_i(x_i)$, the importance sampling estimator $\mathbf{1}\{X \in \mathcal{X}^*\} / g(X)$ of $Q(N)$, with $X$ drawn from $g$, has relative variance at least $\exp\big( N \log N - d - \log Q(N) \big) - 1$, with equality in the exponent at the product of the marginals of $\pi^*$. The crude estimator from the uniform distribution on $[N]^N$ has relative variance $\exp\big( N \log N - \log Q(N) \big) - 1$, so no product proposal reduces the relative second moment (one plus the relative variance) of crude Monte Carlo by more than the factor $e^{d}$.
results.label: thm:product

results.name: Mixing of the reflected Laplace walk of log ordinates
results.summary: Under exactness hypotheses, the chain of log ordinates of the weighted slice sampler is modelled by a reflected Laplace walk that mixes in time quadratic in the log of the rare event probability, quadratic in N for the queens.
results.statement: Assume that the draws of $u \mid x$ and of $x \mid u$ are exact and that $Z(\cdot)$ is known exactly. Use the truncated weight $W = 1/\max\{\eta, Z\}$, with $\eta = \rho$ for a rare event of probability $\rho$, and put $v_{max} = \log(1/\eta)$. While $v_n = -\log Z(L(X_n))$ lies in $[0, v_{max}]$ the chain of log ordinates moves as a symmetric random walk with Laplace increments. Model the chain by this walk reflected at $0$ and $v_{max}$. Then the mixing time of the reflected walk from a warm start to within total variation $\epsilon$ is $O( v_{max}^2 \log(1/\epsilon) )$, which for a rare event of probability $\rho$ is $O( \log^2(1/\rho) \log(1/\epsilon) )$, and for the $N$ queens on permutations is $O( N^2 \log(1/\epsilon) )$. The book does not prove this; its argument is a heuristic.
results.label: conj:reflectedmix

results.name: Vertical likelihood Monte Carlo is polynomial given polynomial level set draws
results.summary: Granted a polynomially convergent adaptive estimate of the curve Z, vertical likelihood Monte Carlo runs in polynomial time exactly when the restricted prior draws on likelihood level sets do, and for the queens exactly when NP equals RP.
results.statement: Suppose the adaptive estimate of $Z(\cdot)$ converges in polynomially many steps, and suppose $\rho > 0$ (for $\rho = 0$ a stopping rule is needed, and for the queens $\log(1/\rho)$ may be replaced by its upper bound $\log N!$ when $\rho > 0$). Vertical likelihood Monte Carlo with the weight $W = 1/\max\{\eta, Z\}$ estimates $Z$ to relative error $\epsilon$ with probability $\tfrac34$ using a number of weighted slice steps polynomial in $\log(1/\rho)$ and $\epsilon^{-1}$, which is expected to be of order $\log^2(1/\rho) \cdot \epsilon^{-2}$ up to a further factor of $\log(1/\rho)$ from the stratified bound, each requiring one draw from the prior restricted to a likelihood level set within total variation of exact equal to $\epsilon$ divided by the number of steps. The algorithm runs in polynomial time if and only if those restricted draws do. In particular, for log concave $L$ and $p$ it runs in polynomial time by Frieze, Kannan and Polson (1994), and for the queens completion count it runs in polynomial time if and only if $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$, by the main equivalence.
results.label: conj:vlpoly

results.name: Riemann sums on random grids for monotone integrands
results.summary: For any monotone integrand the left and right Riemann sums on ordered uniform nodes have mean squared error of order log squared n over n squared, with no smoothness assumed.
results.statement: For any nonincreasing $\Lambda$ on $[0,1]$ with $\Lambda(0) < \infty$, the left and right Riemann sums $\hat Z$ on $n$ ordered uniforms satisfy $\mathbb{E} ( \hat Z - Z )^2 \le ( \Lambda(0) - \Lambda(1) )^2 \, \mathbb{E} ( \max_i D_i )^2 = O( \log^2 n / n^2 )$, where $Z = \int_0^1 \Lambda$ and $D_i$ are the spacings between consecutive nodes, including the endpoints $0$ and $1$.
results.label: thm:riemannmono

results.name: Trapezoid rule on random nodes for Lipschitz and bounded variation integrands
results.summary: The trapezoid rule on ordered uniform nodes has mean squared error of order 1 over n squared for Lipschitz integrands and of order log squared n over n squared for bounded variation or monotone integrands.
results.statement: Let $Z = \int_0^1 \Lambda(s) \, ds$, and let $\hat Z_T$ be the trapezoidal rule on $n$ ordered independent uniform nodes together with the endpoints $0$ and $1$. If $\Lambda$ is Lipschitz with constant $C_1$, then $\mathbb{E} (\hat Z_T - Z)^2 \le 3 C_1^2 / (2 (n+2)^2)$. If $\Lambda$ is of bounded variation $V$, then $\mathbb{E} (\hat Z_T - Z)^2 = O(V^2 \log^2 n / n^2)$, and for monotone $\Lambda$ the same holds with $V = |\Lambda(1) - \Lambda(0)|$.
results.label: thm:lipbv

results.name: Bracketing Riemann sums and trapezoid for a staircase with K jumps
results.summary: For a staircase with K jumps the left and right Riemann sums bracket the integral and have mean squared error at most a constant times lambda one squared K squared over n squared, which Chapter 37 later improves.
results.statement: For a nonincreasing staircase $\Lambda$ with $K$ jumps and values $\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > \dots > \lambda_{K+1} \ge 0$, so that $\Lambda(0) = \lambda_1$, the left and right Riemann sums $\hat Z_L$ and $\hat Z_R$ on the random grid of $n$ ordered uniforms bracket $Z = \int_0^1 \Lambda$ and satisfy $\mathbb{E} (\hat Z_L - Z)^2 \le \mathbb{E} (\hat Z_L - \hat Z_R)^2 \le \frac{6 \lambda_1^2 \, K^2}{(n+1)(n+2)}$, and the trapezoidal rule satisfies the same bound with the constant halved. The error is $O(K \lambda_1 / n)$ in root mean square.
results.label: thm:staircasebracket

results.name: Degree k interpolatory rules on random grids
results.summary: For an integrand with k plus one bounded derivatives, the degree k interpolatory rule on a random grid has mean squared error of order n to the minus 2(k+1).
results.statement: On the random grid $0 = U_{(0)} < U_{(1)} < \dots < U_{(n+1)} = 1$ of $n$ ordered uniforms, a degree $k$ interpolatory rule approximates $\int_{U_{(i-1)}}^{U_{(i)}} \Lambda$ by the integral of the polynomial of degree $k$ that interpolates $\Lambda$ at $k + 1$ consecutive grid points including the endpoints of the cell. Let $\Lambda \in C^{k+1}[0, 1]$ with $\|\Lambda^{(k+1)}\|_\infty \le C_{k+1}$, let $Z = \int_0^1 \Lambda$ and let $\hat Z_k$ be the degree $k$ interpolatory rule on the random grid. Then $\mathbb{E} | \hat Z_k - Z | \le c_k \, C_{k+1} \, n^{-(k+1)}$ and $\mathbb{E} ( \hat Z_k - Z )^2 \le c_k' \, C_{k+1}^2 \, n^{-2(k+1)}$ for constants $c_k, c_k'$ depending only on $k$.
results.label: thm:interp

results.name: Stratified quadrature in the quantile coordinate
results.summary: The stratified estimator, with one uniform node in each of n equal strata, is unbiased with variance bounded by the oscillations on the strata, giving root mean square error of order the square root of K over n for a staircase with K jumps.
results.statement: Let $U_i$ be uniform on the $i$th of $n$ equal strata of $[0,1]$ and let $\hat Z_S = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \Lambda(U_i)$ be the stratified estimator of $Z = \int_0^1 \Lambda$. Then $\hat Z_S$ is unbiased for every integrable $\Lambda$, and $\mathrm{Var} (\hat Z_S) = \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathrm{Var} ( \Lambda(U_i) ) \le \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{ \mathrm{osc}_i(\Lambda)^2 }{4}$, where $\mathrm{osc}_i$ is the oscillation of $\Lambda$ on the $i$th stratum. In particular, for a nonincreasing staircase with $K$ jumps and values $\lambda_1 > \dots > \lambda_{K+1} \ge 0$, $\mathbb{E} (\hat Z_S - Z)^2 \le \frac{K \lambda_1^2}{4 n^2}$, and for Lipschitz $\Lambda$ with constant $C_1$, $\mathbb{E} (\hat Z_S - Z)^2 \le C_1^2 / (4 n^3)$.
results.label: thm:stratified

results.name: Exact mean and variance of the nested sampling estimate under the product Beta law
results.summary: With the discarded likelihoods held fixed and the latent positions following the product Beta law, the nested sampling estimate has an exact mean and an exact variance formula given by second moments of the positions.
results.statement: Let $n$ be the number of live points, let the latent positions be $s_k = \prod_{j=1}^{k} t_j$ with $t_j$ independent of law $\mathrm{Beta}(n, 1)$ (the maximum of $n$ uniforms), and set $s_0 = 1$. Hold the discarded likelihood sequence $(y_k)$ fixed. Then the nested sampling estimate $\hat Z = \sum_k y_k (s_{k-1} - s_k)$ has, under the law of the positions, $\mathbb{E} \hat Z = \sum_{k \ge 1} y_k \, \frac{1}{n+1} \big( \frac{n}{n+1} \big)^{k-1}$ and $\mathrm{Var} \hat Z = \sum_{k, l} y_k y_l \, \mathrm{Cov}(s_{k-1} - s_k, \, s_{l-1} - s_l)$, where $\mathbb{E} s_k = (n/(n+1))^k$, $\mathbb{E} s_k^2 = (n/(n+2))^k$, and for $k \le l$, $\mathbb{E} s_k s_l = (n/(n+2))^k (n/(n+1))^{l-k}$.
results.label: thm:nestedmoments

results.name: Trapezoid error as an integral against the jump measure
results.summary: The error of the trapezoidal rule on random ordered nodes equals the integral of the signed distance to the midpoint of the containing spacing against the jump measure of the integrand.
results.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be of bounded variation on $[0,1]$, right continuous on $(0,1)$, and let $\mu = -d\Lambda$ be the signed measure on $(0,1)$ with $\Lambda(s) = \Lambda(1) + \mu((s,1))$ and total variation $V$. Let $U_{(1)} < \dots < U_{(n)}$ be the order statistics of $n$ independent uniform variables on $[0,1]$, with $U_{(0)}=0$ and $U_{(n+1)}=1$, let $\hat Z_T$ be the trapezoidal rule for $Z=\int_0^1 \Lambda(s)\,ds$ on these nodes, let $A(s)=s-\max\{U_{(i)} \le s\}$ and $B(s)=\min\{U_{(i)}>s\}-s$ be the distances from $s$ to the nodes on either side, and let $D(s)=(B(s)-A(s))/2$. Then, almost surely, $\hat Z_T - Z = \int_0^1 D(s)\,\mu(ds)$.
results.label: thm:errrep

results.name: Moments of the spacing containing a fixed point
results.summary: The signed distance from a fixed point to the midpoint of its spacing among uniform nodes has an explicit mean and second moment, bounded by one over twice n plus one and one over twice (n+1)(n+2).
results.statement: With $A(s)$, $B(s)$ and $D(s)=(B(s)-A(s))/2$ defined from $n$ independent uniform nodes on $[0,1]$ as the distances from $s$ to the nearest node on its left and on its right (with $0$ and $1$ added as nodes), for fixed $s\in(0,1)$ one has $\mathbb{P}(A(s)>a,\,B(s)>b)=(1-a-b)^n$ for $0\le a<s$, $0\le b<1-s$, $a+b\le 1$. Consequently $\mathbb{E}D(s)=\frac{(1-s)^{n+1}-s^{n+1}}{2(n+1)}$ and $\mathbb{E}D(s)^2=\frac{1-(n+2)\,s(1-s)\big(s^n+(1-s)^n\big)}{2(n+1)(n+2)}$. In particular $|\mathbb{E}D(s)|\le \frac{1}{2(n+1)}$ and $\mathbb{E}D(s)^2\le\frac{1}{2(n+1)(n+2)}$, the second attained asymptotically at every interior $s$.
results.label: lem:spacing

results.name: Exact bias and mean squared error of the trapezoid on one step
results.summary: For an integrand with a single jump, the bias and mean squared error of the trapezoidal rule on random ordered nodes are given in closed form, with leading mean squared error h squared over 2 n squared.
results.statement: Let $\Lambda=\lambda_1$ on $[0,p)$ and $\Lambda=\lambda_2$ on $[p,1]$, a single step of height $h=\lambda_1-\lambda_2$ at $p\in(0,1)$, and let $\hat Z_T$ be the trapezoidal rule on $n$ independent uniform nodes ordered, with endpoints $0$ and $1$ included, for $Z=\int_0^1\Lambda$. Then $\mathbb{E}(\hat Z_T-Z)=h\,\frac{(1-p)^{n+1}-p^{n+1}}{2(n+1)}$ and $\mathbb{E}(\hat Z_T-Z)^2=h^2\,\frac{1-(n+2)\,p(1-p)\big(p^n+(1-p)^n\big)}{2(n+1)(n+2)}$.
results.label: thm:onestep

results.name: Trapezoid on random nodes for bounded variation, no logarithm
results.summary: For any integrand of bounded variation V the trapezoid on random ordered nodes has bias at most V over 2(n+1) and mean squared error at most V squared over 2(n+1)(n+2), with no logarithm and no dependence on the number of steps.
results.statement: Let $\Lambda$ have total variation $V$ on $[0,1]$ and let $\hat Z_T$ be the trapezoidal rule on $n$ independent uniform nodes, ordered, with the endpoints $0$ and $1$ included, for $Z=\int_0^1\Lambda$. Then $|\mathbb{E}(\hat Z_T-Z)|\le \frac{V}{2(n+1)}$ and $\mathbb{E}(\hat Z_T-Z)^2\le\frac{V^2}{2(n+1)(n+2)}$. For a nonincreasing staircase whose jumps all lie in $[\delta,1-\delta]$ the bias is at most $\frac{V(1-\delta)^{n+1}}{2(n+1)}$.
results.label: thm:bv

results.name: Asymptotic constant of the trapezoid for separated steps
results.summary: For a staircase with fixed separated jumps the mean squared error of the trapezoid is the sum of squared jump heights over 2 n squared, up to a relative error of order one over n.
results.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be a staircase with jumps of heights $h_1,\dots,h_K$ at fixed interior locations, and let $\hat Z_T$ be the trapezoidal rule on $n$ independent uniform nodes, ordered, with the endpoints included. Then $\mathbb{E}(\hat Z_T-Z)^2=\frac{\sum_k h_k^2}{2n^2}\big(1+O(1/n)\big)$, where the constant in the $O$ depends on $K$ and on the minimum gap between jumps.
results.label: prop:asym

results.name: Stratified midpoint rule variance bound free of the number of steps
results.summary: The stratified rule on n strata has variance at most V squared over 4 n squared for bounded variation V, and sum of squared jump heights over 4 n squared for a staircase with at most one jump per stratum.
results.statement: Let $\hat Z_S=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\Lambda(U_i)$ with $U_i$ uniform on the $i$th of $n$ equal strata of $[0,1]$, independent. For any $\Lambda$ of bounded variation $V$, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat Z_S)\le \frac{V^2}{4n^2}$. For a staircase with jump heights $h_k$ no two of whose jumps lie in the same stratum, $\mathrm{Var}(\hat Z_S)\le\frac{\sum_k h_k^2}{4n^2}$.
results.label: thm:stratbv

results.name: Amortised ladder with a fitted level set generator
results.summary: A ladder run with draws from a fitted level set generator, with equal ratios, has relative mean squared error T(1 - theta)/(theta M) plus a bias term of order T squared delta squared over theta squared, at first order only.
results.statement: Suppose a level set generator $G_\phi(m, \xi)$ is fitted so that for each level $m_t$ the law of $G_\phi(m_t, \xi)$ is within total variation $\delta$ of $P(\cdot \mid S \le m_t)$. Suppose also that the $T$ ratios equal a common value $\theta$. Then the ladder run with $M$ draws from $G_\phi$ at each rung estimates $\rho$ with relative mean squared error, to first order in $T(1 - \theta)/(\theta M)$ and $T\delta/\theta$, at most $T(1 - \theta)/(\theta M) + O(T^2 \delta^2/\theta^2)$, and costs $T M$ evaluations of $G_\phi$ with no Markov chain steps.
results.label: thm:amortised

results.name: Minimal sufficiency of the closure of a board
results.summary: For the queens completion problem the set of squares occupied by every completion is a minimal sufficient statistic, and the posterior mean matrix is sufficient and reveals it as its entries equal to one.
results.statement: Let $X_0$ be a board of $k$ fixed queens in distinct rows and columns, with completion set $C(X_0)$ (the placements of $N$ non attacking queens containing $X_0$) and uniform posterior on $C(X_0)$. Define the closure $\bar X_0=\bigcap_{x\in C(X_0)}x$ and the posterior mean matrix $M(X_0)_{ic}=\mathbb{P}(x_i=c\mid X_0)=N(0;X_0\cup\{(i,c)\})/N(0;X_0)$, where $N(0;\cdot)$ is the number of completions. On boards with at least one completion, $\bar X_0$ is a minimal sufficient statistic for the completion law, and $M(X_0)$ is a sufficient statistic with $\bar X_0=\{(i,c):M(X_0)_{ic}=1\}$.
results.label: thm:closure

results.name: Posterior mean sufficiency for completion problems
results.summary: For any completion problem where fixing a forced value changes nothing, including every self reducible problem, the posterior mean is a sufficient statistic and its entries equal to one form a minimal one.
results.statement: Consider a problem whose instances are partial assignments $X_0$ of variables to values, whose posterior is the uniform law on the complete assignments extending $X_0$ that satisfy a fixed constraint, and suppose that extending a partial assignment by a value assigned in every completion does not change the completion set. Then the posterior mean, the vector of probabilities $\mathbb{P}(\text{variable } i=v\mid X_0)$, is a sufficient statistic for the posterior, and the set of its entries equal to one is minimal sufficient.
results.label: thm:pmean

results.name: Hardness of the closure and the posterior mean matrix
results.summary: Deciding membership in the closure is coNP hard, the exact posterior mean matrix is sharp P hard, and approximating it to relative accuracy one over N squared is possible in randomized polynomial time if and only if NP equals RP.
results.statement: Extend the closure to boards with forbidden squares, and to boards with no completion by declaring every square to be in the closure of such a board. Deciding whether a given square belongs to the closure is then $\mathrm{coNP}$ hard. Computing the posterior mean matrix exactly is $\#\mathrm{P}$ hard. A randomized polynomial time algorithm that approximates every entry of the matrix within a factor $1\pm1/N^2$ on every board exists if and only if $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}$.
results.label: thm:cost

results.name: Learned generators conditioning on a summary statistic
results.summary: A generator that is exactly uniform on completions given a summary forces the summary to be sufficient, a polynomial time version would give NP equal to RP, and a generator that is a product over rows pays at least the mean field gap.
results.statement: Let $T$ be any statistic of the board and $G(\tau,T(X_0))$ a generator, a measurable function of base noise $\tau$ and the statistic, whose output law is uniform on the completion set $C(X_0)$ for every board. Then $T$ is sufficient for the completion law, and hence determines the closure. If in addition $G$ is computable in polynomial time and $T$ is computable in randomized polynomial time with error probability at most $1/4$, then $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}$. If $T$ is the posterior mean matrix $M$ and $G(\tau,M)=(G_1(\tau_1,M_{1\cdot}),\dots,G_N(\tau_N,M_{N\cdot}))$ has independent coordinates, then the divergence of the uniform completion law from the output law $P_G$ of $G$ satisfies $D(\pi(\cdot\mid X_0)\,\|\,P_G)\ge\sum_i H_i-\log N(0;X_0)$, where $H_i$ is the entropy of row $i$ of $M(X_0)$ and $N(0;X_0)$ is the number of completions; for the unconditioned problem this mean field gap equals $\alpha N-d+o(N)$, where $\alpha$ is the constant in $Q(N)=\big((1+o(1))Ne^{-\alpha}\big)^N$ and $d=\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\log N-H_i)$ is the entropy deficit of the row entropies on the empty board, so it is linear in $N$ if $d/N$ stays below $\alpha$.
results.label: thm:gbcsuff

results.name: Planted sampling gives the posterior mean but weights boards by completions
results.summary: Training on planted pairs of a uniform solution and a random subset of its queens makes the posterior mean the regression target, but the training boards appear in proportion to their number of completions, so hard boards are rarely seen.
results.statement: Draw a uniform solution $x$ of the $N$ queens problem, of which there are $Q(N)$, draw a uniform $k$ subset of its rows, and keep the queens of $x$ in those rows as the board $X_0$; write $P_k$ for the joint law of $(x,X_0)$. Under $P_k$ the conditional law of $x$ given $X_0$ is the uniform law on the completion set $C(X_0)$, so the regression function $\mathbb{E}_{P_k}[\mathbf 1\{x_i=c\}\mid X_0]$ is the posterior mean matrix $M(X_0)$, and the population minimiser of the squared loss under $P_k$ is $M(X_0)$ on every board with a completion. The marginal law of the board is $P_k(X_0)=\frac{N(0;X_0)}{Q(N)\binom{N}{k}}$, where $N(0;X_0)$ is the number of completions of $X_0$, so that a board is seen with probability proportional to its number of completions and the expected number of planted pairs needed to see a given board once is $Q(N)\binom Nk/N(0;X_0)$.
results.label: thm:planted

results.name: Learning the posterior mean matrix is equivalent to NP equals RP
results.summary: NP equals RP is equivalent to a randomized polynomial time algorithm, or a uniform polynomial size circuit family, computing the queens posterior mean matrix of every board to relative accuracy one over N squared.
results.statement: The following are equivalent. (1) $\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{RP}$. (2) There is a randomized algorithm which, given any board $X_0$ with completions, outputs in time polynomial in $N$ a matrix $\tilde M$ with $\tilde M_{ic}\in(1\pm1/N^2)M(X_0)_{ic}$ for every entry, where $M(X_0)$ is the posterior mean matrix of the uniform completion law, with probability at least $3/4$. (3) There is a uniform family of circuits $C_N$ of size polynomial in $N$, produced from $N$ by a polynomial time algorithm, which, given a board $X_0$ with completions and a random string, outputs such a matrix with probability at least $3/4$.
results.label: thm:jwequiv

results.name: Conditional FPRAS for the vertical walk with stratified quadrature
results.status_text: conditional on a level set sampler producing, in time C(N, delta), a sample within total variation delta of uniform on every sublevel set; the ladder hypothesis, that the ladder has at most 2K rungs and consecutive rung size ratios at least one half; for the optimality remark only, for the optimality remark only, that relative error epsilon in the product requires relative error of order epsilon over the square root of K in each rung ratio, which the book assumes and does not prove
results.conditions: a level set sampler producing, in time C(N, delta), a sample within total variation delta of uniform on every sublevel set; the ladder hypothesis, that the ladder has at most 2K rungs and consecutive rung size ratios at least one half; for the optimality remark only, for the optimality remark only, that relative error epsilon in the product requires relative error of order epsilon over the square root of K in each rung ratio, which the book assumes and does not prove
results.summary: Given a level set sampler and a ladder of at most 2K rungs with ratios at least one half, the vertical walk with stratified quadrature approximates the ground state count in time K squared over epsilon squared times the sampler cost, so counting reduces to level set sampling.
results.statement: Let $S$ be an energy on a finite set $\mathcal{X}$ of known size, taking at most $K + 1$ values with $N(0) > 0$, and suppose a level set sampler is available that produces, in time $C(N, \delta)$, a sample within total variation $\delta$ of uniform on $\{ S \le m \}$ for any $m$. Suppose also that the ladder of level sets used by the walk has at most $2K$ rungs and that consecutive rungs have size ratio at least $\tfrac12$. Then for any $\epsilon \in (0, 1)$ the vertical walk with stratified quadrature produces an estimate $\hat N(0)$ of the ground state count with $\mathbb{P}( |\hat N(0) / N(0) - 1| > \epsilon ) \le \tfrac14$, in time $O\big( \frac{K^2}{\epsilon^2} \cdot C(N, \epsilon / K) \big)$, and for estimators that estimate each rung ratio separately the dependence on $K$ and $\epsilon$ cannot be improved by more than logarithmic factors (the book does not prove a lower bound for arbitrary estimators).
results.label: thm:condfpras

results.name: FPRAS for the unconditioned queens count under mixing hypotheses (sketch)
results.status_text: conditional on the sublevel set of energy at most 2 is connected under swaps; polynomial mixing time of the swap chain on every sublevel set of energy at most m for every m at least 2; consecutive ratios of the sublevel sets on the integer ladder are at least inverse polynomial in N; polynomial mixing of the swap chain on the giant component of the sublevel set of energy at most 1, with a membership test and with the giant component holding all but an N to the minus c fraction of the solutions; closing the two gaps the book names in its proof sketch (ratios only inverse polynomial instead of at least one half, and no bound on the size of the giant component relative to the sublevel set)
results.conditions: the sublevel set of energy at most 2 is connected under swaps; polynomial mixing time of the swap chain on every sublevel set of energy at most m for every m at least 2; consecutive ratios of the sublevel sets on the integer ladder are at least inverse polynomial in N; polynomial mixing of the swap chain on the giant component of the sublevel set of energy at most 1, with a membership test and with the giant component holding all but an N to the minus c fraction of the solutions; closing the two gaps the book names in its proof sketch (ratios only inverse polynomial instead of at least one half, and no bound on the size of the giant component relative to the sublevel set)
results.summary: Under connectivity and polynomial mixing hypotheses for the swap chain on the unconditioned queens, an FPRAS for the number of solutions would follow; the book gives only a sketch with two acknowledged gaps.
results.statement: Suppose that for the unconditioned $N$ queens problem the level set $\{ S \le 2 \}$ is connected under swaps, that the swap chain on $\{ S \le m \}$ has polynomial mixing time for every $m \ge 2$, that consecutive ratios $|\{ S \le m-1 \}| / |\{ S \le m \}|$ on the integer ladder are at least inverse polynomial in $N$, and that the swap chain on the giant component $G$ of $\{ S \le 1 \}$ has polynomial mixing time, with a membership test for $G$ and with $G$ holding a $1 - O(N^{-c})$ fraction of the solutions for some $c > 0$ (small $N$ being handled by enumeration). Then there is an FPRAS for $Q(N)$, the number of solutions of the $N$ queens problem. The last hypothesis can be dropped at the cost of replacing the bottom rung by the direct Bernoulli estimate of $Q(N) / |\{ S \le 2 \}|$, which is polynomial if that ratio is at least inverse polynomial.
results.label: prop:fpras_unconditioned

results.name: An RP language is decided by the median of the quantile function of its algorithm
results.summary: Deciding a language in RP is the same as evaluating at one half the quantile function of the acceptance probability of its algorithm, that is, taking a median.
results.statement: Let $L \in \mathrm{RP}$ with an algorithm $A$ that accepts every $x \in L$ with probability $p(x) > \tfrac12$ (one round of amplification gives one), and never accepts $x \notin L$. Let $\Lambda_x$ be the quantile function of the algorithm on input $x$, the step function equal to $1$ for $s < p(x)$ and $0$ otherwise. Then for every input $x$, $x \in L$ if and only if $\Lambda_x(\tfrac12) = \operatorname{med}_r A(x, r) = 1$, where the median is over a uniform random string $r$.
results.label: prop:median

results.name: P = RP if and only if medians of RP type Boolean functions are computable in P
results.summary: P equals RP exactly when the median can be computed deterministically in polynomial time for every polynomial time Boolean function that, on every input, is either identically zero or true on more than half of the random strings.
results.statement: $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{RP}$ if and only if the following holds. For every polynomial time computable Boolean function $f(x, r)$, $r \in \{0,1\}^{m(|x|)}$, such that for every $x$ either $f(x, \cdot) \equiv 0$ or $\mathbb{P}_r(f(x, r) = 1) > \tfrac12$, the median $\operatorname{med}_r f(x, r)$ is computable in deterministic polynomial time.
results.label: thm:medians

results.name: Conditional FPRAS with an integer ladder from a polynomial level set sampler
results.status_text: conditional on a polynomial level set sampler for the energy; every ratio of consecutive level sets is at least 1/q for a polynomial q
results.conditions: a polynomial level set sampler for the energy; every ratio of consecutive level sets is at least 1/q for a polynomial q
results.summary: A polynomial level set sampler together with inverse polynomial ratios of consecutive level sets gives an FPRAS for the ground state count by running the vertical walk on the integer ladder.
results.statement: Let $S : \mathcal{X} \to \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$ be an energy on a finite set $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|$ known and $K$ polynomial in the input size. Say that $S$ admits a polynomial level set sampler if there is a randomized polynomial time procedure which, given a level $m$ and an accuracy $\delta$, produces a sample from the uniform distribution on $\{ x : S(x) \le m \}$ to within total variation $\delta$ in time polynomial in the input size and $\log(1/\delta)$. If $S$ admits a polynomial level set sampler, and every ratio $Z_{t-1} / Z_t$ of consecutive level sets is at least $1/q$ for a polynomial $q$, then there is an FPRAS for $N(0) = \#\{ x : S(x) = 0 \}$, and hence for every cumulative count $\#\{ x : S(x) \le s \}$. The FPRAS runs the vertical likelihood walk with the ladder $m_t = t$ for $t = K, K-1, \dots, 0$, estimating each ratio $Z_{t-1} / Z_t$ by $O(K q / \epsilon^2)$ conditioned samples at level $t$, for a total of $O(K^2 q \, \epsilon^{-2})$ samples.
results.label: thm:vertical_condfpras

results.name: A polynomial level set sampler for the queens energy gives NP = RP
results.status_text: conditional on a polynomial level set sampler for the queens energy on partially filled boards; the ratios of consecutive level sets of the queens energy are at least inverse polynomial
results.conditions: a polynomial level set sampler for the queens energy on partially filled boards; the ratios of consecutive level sets of the queens energy are at least inverse polynomial
results.summary: If the queens energy on partial boards admitted a polynomial level set sampler with inverse polynomial rung ratios, there would be an FPRAS for the completion count and hence NP would equal RP.
results.statement: If the queens energy, the number of attacking pairs on a partially filled board, admits a polynomial level set sampler, and the ratios of consecutive level sets are at least inverse polynomial, then there is an FPRAS for the queens completion count, and therefore $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$.
results.label: cor:queens_nprp

results.name: Vertical form of the queens conjecture
results.summary: The queens energy on partial boards is conjectured to admit no polynomial level set sampler, so that every polynomial time ergodic chain on its level sets mixes superpolynomially somewhere; this is NP differs from RP specialised to the queens.
results.statement: The queens energy on partial boards does not admit a polynomial level set sampler. In particular, every Markov chain on partial queens placements whose transitions are computable in polynomial time and which is ergodic on each level set $\{ S \le m \}$ has mixing time superpolynomial in $N$ for some $m$ and some partial board.
results.label: conj:queens_vertical

results.name: The block chain is reversible and irreducible when the level set is connected
results.summary: The block swap chain with exact conditional resampling of each block is reversible with respect to the uniform law on the level set and irreducible whenever the level set is connected under the allowed block moves.
results.statement: The block chain with binomially distributed block size and exact resampling of each block conditional on the level set is reversible with respect to the uniform distribution on the level set, and is irreducible on it whenever the level set is connected under moves that permute any $k$ rows at once for $k$ up to the maximal block size attained.
results.label: prop:blockvalid

results.name: Mixing of the block chain on unconditioned and reduction boards
results.summary: The block chain on the bottom level set is conjectured to mix in polynomial time on the unconditioned queens and superpolynomially on boards from the reduction applied to hard satisfiability instances.
results.statement: Let $q$ be the probability with which each row is included in the random block. For the block chain on $\{ S \le 1 \}$ for the unconditioned $N$ queens problem, the mixing time is polynomial in $N$ for every constant $q \in (0, 1)$. For the block chain on $\{ S \le 1 \}$ for the completion problem with partial placements drawn from the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction applied to hard satisfiability instances, the mixing time is superpolynomial for every $q$ bounded away from one.
results.label: conj:blockmix

results.name: Polynomial mixing of the swap chain on the bottom level set of the queens
results.summary: The swap chain restricted to the giant component of the permutations with at most one attacking pair is conjectured to mix in polynomial time, with the giant component holding almost all solutions.
results.statement: Let $S(x)$ be the number of attacking pairs of queens in the permutation $x \in S_N$, let $A_N = \{ x \in S_N : S(x) \le 1 \}$, and let $G_N$ be the connected component of $A_N$, under swaps of two rows, that contains the most solutions (permutations with $S(x) = 0$). The swap chain on $G_N$ chooses a pair of rows uniformly among the $\binom{N}{2}$ pairs, swaps their columns to get $y$, and moves to $y$ if $S(y) \le 1$ and otherwise stays. Conjecture: there is a constant $c$ such that for all $N \ge 8$ the swap chain on $G_N$ has mixing time at most $N^c$. Moreover $|G_N \cap \{ S = 0 \}| \ge (1 - o(1))\, Q(N)$, where $Q(N)$ is the number of solutions of the $N$ queens problem.
results.label: conj:mixing

results.name: Reversibility, irreducibility and aperiodicity of the swap chain on the giant component
results.summary: The swap chain on the giant component is reversible with respect to the uniform law, irreducible and aperiodic from N equal to 8, with off diagonal transition probabilities zero or one over the number of pairs.
results.statement: The swap chain on $G_N$, the connected component of $\{ x \in S_N : S(x) \le 1 \}$ under swaps of two rows that contains the most solutions, with moves given by swapping the columns of two rows chosen uniformly among the $\binom{N}{2}$ pairs and rejecting moves that leave the set, is reversible with respect to the uniform distribution on $G_N$, is irreducible on $G_N$ by the definition of $G_N$, and is aperiodic for $N \ge 8$. Its off diagonal transition probabilities are $0$ or $1 / \binom{N}{2}$.
results.label: lem:chainfacts

results.name: A swap of a solution creates at most four attacks
results.summary: Swapping two rows of a solution of the N queens problem leaves at most four attacking pairs.
results.statement: Let $x$ be a solution of the $N$ queens problem, a permutation with $S(x) = 0$ attacking pairs, and let $y$ be obtained from $x$ by swapping the columns of two rows $i$ and $j$. Then $S(y) \le 4$.
results.label: lem:four

results.name: Expansion of the bottom level set
results.summary: The swap graph on the giant component of the near solutions has conductance bounded below by an inverse polynomial in N, which is equivalent to polynomial mixing of the swap chain.
results.statement: Let $S(x)$ be the number of attacking pairs of queens in $x \in S_N$, let $G_N$ be the connected component of $\{ x \in S_N : S(x) \le 1 \}$, under swaps of two rows, that contains the most solutions, and let $\Phi_N$ be the conductance of the swap chain on $G_N$, that is, the minimum over subsets $A \subseteq G_N$ with $|A| \le |G_N|/2$ of the number of swap edges leaving $A$ divided by $\binom{N}{2} |A|$. Conjecture: there is a constant $c'$ such that $\Phi_N \ge N^{-c'}$ for all $N \ge 8$.
results.label: conj:expansion

results.name: Expansion of the bottom level set is equivalent to polynomial mixing
results.summary: By Cheeger's inequality, a polynomial lower bound on the conductance of the giant component gives polynomial mixing of the lazy swap chain, and polynomial mixing conversely gives the conductance bound.
results.statement: Let $G_N$ be the connected component of $\{ x \in S_N : S(x) \le 1 \}$, under swaps of two rows, that contains the most solutions of the $N$ queens problem, where $S(x)$ is the number of attacking pairs, and let $\Phi_N$ be the conductance of the swap chain on $G_N$, the minimum over $A \subseteq G_N$ with $|A| \le |G_N|/2$ of the number of swap edges leaving $A$ divided by $\binom{N}{2} |A|$. If $\Phi_N \ge N^{-c'}$ for all $N \ge 8$, then the lazy version of the swap chain has mixing time $\tau(\epsilon) \le \frac{4}{\Phi_N^2} \big( N \log N + \log(1/\epsilon) \big) \le 4 N^{2c'} \big( N \log N + \log(1/\epsilon) \big)$, where $\tau(\epsilon)$ is the time to reach total variation distance $\epsilon$ from the uniform distribution on $G_N$. Conversely, if the swap chain on $G_N$ has mixing time at most $N^c$ for all $N \ge 8$, then $\Phi_N \ge N^{-(c+1)}$, so the expansion bound holds with $c' = c + 1$.
results.label: thm:reduction

results.name: The main equivalence, NP = RP if and only if queens completions can be sampled or counted in polynomial time
results.summary: NP equals RP exactly when the completions of a partial queens placement can be sampled almost uniformly, the level sets of the queens energy can be sampled, or the number of completions can be approximated, in randomized polynomial time.
results.statement: The following are equivalent. (1) $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$. (2) There is a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler for the completions of a partial queens placement. That is, there is a randomized algorithm which, given $(N, X_0)$ and $\delta > 0$, outputs in time polynomial in $N$ and $\log(1/\delta)$ a placement whose law is within total variation $\delta$ of uniform on the set of completions, or reports correctly that there are none. (3) There is a fully polynomial almost uniform sampler which, given $(N, X_0, m)$ and $\delta > 0$, samples the level set $\{ x : S(x) \le m, \, x \supseteq X_0 \}$ of the queens energy $S$ on partial boards, in time polynomial in $N$ and $\log(1/\delta)$, uniformly in $m$. (4) There is a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number of completions $\#\mathrm{QUEENS}(N, X_0)$.
results.label: thm:mainequiv

results.name: Median form of the hitting set characterisation of prRP = prP
results.status_text: conditional on the extension to promise problems of the Buhrman and Fortnow theorem, that prRP = prP implies prBPP = prP (used only for (1) implies (2))
results.conditions: the extension to promise problems of the Buhrman and Fortnow theorem, that prRP = prP implies prBPP = prP (used only for (1) implies (2))
results.summary: A restatement on the quantile axis of the known hitting set formulation, saying that promise RP equals promise P exactly when a point with value one, or the median, of a polynomial time Boolean function can be found deterministically under the promise. It rests on the Buhrman and Fortnow theorem, assumed here to extend to promise problems.
results.statement: Let $\mathrm{prRP}$ and $\mathrm{prP}$ denote the promise versions of $\mathrm{RP}$ and $\mathrm{P}$, in which an algorithm is required to be correct only on inputs satisfying the promise. The following are equivalent. (1) $\mathrm{prRP} = \mathrm{prP}$. (2) For every polynomial time computable $f : \{0,1\}^* \times \{0,1\}^{m(n)} \to \{0, 1\}$ there is a deterministic polynomial time algorithm which, on input $x$ with $|x| = n$, outputs a point $r$ with $f(x, r) = 1$ whenever $\mathbb{P}_r(f(x, r) = 1) \ge \tfrac12$. (3) For every such $f$ the median of $f(x, \cdot)$ over $r$, defined as $1$ if $\mathbb{P}_r(f(x,r) = 1) \ge \tfrac12$ and $0$ otherwise, is computable in deterministic polynomial time on the promise that either $f(x, \cdot) \equiv 0$ or $\mathbb{P}_r(f(x,r) = 1) \ge \tfrac12$. Moreover (3) restricted to the pairs $(f, x)$ arising from $\mathrm{RP}$ languages is equivalent to $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{RP}$.
results.label: thm:derandequiv

results.name: Limits of Monte Carlo for the queens completion problem
results.summary: No one sided error decision algorithm, polynomial factor approximation of the completion count, or sampler within constant total variation distance runs in polynomial time unless NP equals RP.
results.statement: No randomized algorithm decides $\mathrm{QUEENS}$ with one sided error in polynomial time unless $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$. No randomized algorithm approximates $\#\mathrm{QUEENS}$ to within any polynomial factor in polynomial time unless $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$. No randomized algorithm samples the completions of a partial board to within any constant total variation distance in polynomial time unless $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$.
results.label: thm:limitsmc

results.name: Conditional FPRAS with explicit rates for the stratified vertical walk
results.summary: For an energy with K plus one levels and reversible lazy level set chains with relaxation time at most t star, the stratified vertical walk estimates the ground state count with a number of chain steps given by an explicit bound, assuming the ratios of the product estimator are bounded below.
results.statement: Let $S$ be an energy on a finite set $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|$ known and at most $K + 1$ levels, and let the level set chain at level $m$ be a reversible lazy chain whose stationary law is uniform on the level set, with relaxation time $t_{rel}(m)$. Let $t^* = \max_m t_{rel}(m)$, and assume that the successive ratios $\theta_t$ of the product estimator are bounded below by a constant $\theta_0 > 0$. Then the stratified vertical walk estimates $N(0)$ to relative error $\epsilon$ with probability $\tfrac34$ using at most $O\big( \frac{K^2}{\epsilon^2} \cdot t^* \cdot ( \log |\mathcal{X}| + \log(K / \epsilon) ) \big)$ chain steps, and the quadrature contribution to the root mean squared error is at most $\lambda_1 \sqrt{K} / (2n)$ for $n$ stratified nodes per rung, where $\lambda_1$ is the largest step value of the quantile staircase.
results.label: thm:condfpras_rates

results.name: Rung skipping, the walk that starts at a connected level set
results.status_text: conditional on the swap chain on every sublevel set of energy at most j, for j at least m, is irreducible and mixes in polynomial time T; the rung ratios are at least 1/q(N) for a polynomial q; the ratio of the number of ground states to the size of the sublevel set at m is at least 1/p(N) for a polynomial p

results.summary: If a connected, well mixed sublevel set is reached at some depth m with polynomial rung ratios and a polynomial ground state fraction, the vertical walk need not use the bottom rung and gives an FPRAS for the completion count.
results.statement: Let $B$ be a board with completions and let $m \ge m_c(B)$, where $m_c(B)$ is the shattering depth of $B$. Suppose the swap chain on the conditioned level set $\{ S \le j \}$ is irreducible and mixes in time $T$, polynomial in $N$, for every $j \ge m$, that $|\{ S \le j \}| / |\{ S \le j + 1 \}| \ge 1 / q(N)$ for every $j \ge m$ and a polynomial $q$, and that $N(0) / |\{ S \le m \}| \ge 1 / p(N)$ for a polynomial $p$. Let $K$ be the number of rungs above $m$, that is, the number of $j \ge m$ with $\{ S \le j \}$ not the whole board. Then the vertical walk that estimates $N(0) / |\{ S \le m \}|$ directly, as the fraction of ground states among samples from $\{ S \le m \}$, and the ratios $|\{ S \le j \}| / |\{ S \le j + 1 \}|$ for $j \ge m$ by the product estimator, is an FPRAS for the completion count with cost $O((K^3 q(N) + p(N)) \epsilon^{-2} T \log (K/\delta))$ for confidence $1 - \delta$.
results.label: thm:rungskip

results.name: Shattering depth on hard boards
results.summary: On boards built from hard formulas by the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction the shattering depth is conjectured to grow linearly in N, so that the ground state ratio at that depth is exponentially small.
results.statement: There is a family of boards $B_N$ from the Gent, Jefferson and Nightingale reduction applied to hard formulas with $m_c(B_N) \ge c N$ for a constant $c > 0$, where $m_c(B_N)$ is the shattering depth, and for such boards the ratio $N(0) / |\{ S \le m_c(B_N) \}|$ is exponentially small in $N$.
results.label: conj:shatterdepth

results.name: Depth growth on random boards
results.summary: On random boards with a fixed number of fixed queens the shattering depth is conjectured to stay bounded, so that the price of rung skipping is inverse polynomial, against the alternatives of logarithmic or linear growth.
results.statement: On random boards with a fixed number of fixed queens, $m_c(B) = O(1)$ with high probability, so that the price of rung skipping is inverse polynomial. The data to $N = 16$ do not exclude slow growth, since $m_c(B) = O(\log N)$ would make the price quasi polynomial, and the alternative, $m_c(B) \ge cN$, would make the vertical walk exponential on random boards.
results.label: conj:depthgrowth
